title: With a New Strategy, Be Sure the Old Structures Still Support It
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Argues that leaders who adopt a new strategy must also adjust the existing structures that will carry it, such as reporting lines, processes, technology, reward systems, and metrics. Leaving old structures in place is easy and tempting, but without alignment the strategy is unlikely to take hold. The author gives examples such as changing a sales strategy without changing compensation, or launching a new product strategy without updating marketing processes. A list of often-overlooked structures follows, from governance to feedback mechanisms. The post singles out the reward system as the most important structure, summarizing the principle that what gets rewarded gets done.
points: A strategy change is incomplete until reporting lines, processes, technology, rewards, and metrics are realigned to it.
Common failure: changing a sales or product strategy while leaving compensation, marketing processes, or technology untouched.
Misaligned structures can leave the organization worse off than before the new strategy.
The reward system is the most decisive structure: without aligned rewards a new strategy is doomed.
Leaders always get what they reward, so rewards must advance the specific differences they want to see.
quotes: In today’s fast-moving marketplace, changes in strategy happen quickly. Leaders frequently craft a new strategy to take full advantage of the changes and opportunities they see or to overcome problems that have been hindering growth or effectiveness.

It is just too easy for leaders to leave many of the former structures in place without thinking through the consequences of such a choice. Without the correct structures to support the new strategy, the odds are against it taking hold in the organization or making a difference.

For instance, leaders often change a sales strategy without concurrently altering the compensation system that will drive the new sales tactics. Or they craft a new product or service strategy without incorporating changes into marketing processes or technology usage that will increase the probability of success.

Strategies without the underlying structures that encourage internal acceptance and reinforce the desired outcomes leave the organization worse off. Structures are the building blocks for strategy success and need to be considered before any new strategy is executed.

But among the many structures essential to strategy success, perhaps none is more important than the reward system that supports it. Without the appropriate rewards that align with the desired strategic outcomes, the new strategy is doomed to fail.

What gets rewarded in organizations is what gets done. Good leaders never change a strategy without ensuring that the reward and recognition scheme advances the differences they hope to see. Leaders always get what they reward.
